1.5 — Movement II: Speed, deltaTime & Tuning

Your character moves, and one thing about that is wrong: hold two direction keys at once and it travels 41% faster. Today you measure that, name the one line that fixes it, and then make a decision about it — which is not the same thing as failing to fix it.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“why does my character move faster diagonally, and how do I fix it?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

My character moves faster on the diagonal than in a straight line. The movement from 1.4 already works, and that is what makes the wrongness hard to see.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Keep the two axes apart instead of multiplying on the move lineTwo fields, xVector and yVector, filled from the two reads you already have. The same product as 1.4, written where the rest of the course can read it.Read: the field declarations from 1.3, and the two reads from 1.4.
  2. Prove that a frame is not a secondRun the game at two very different frame rates and watch the character cross the same ground in the same real time. That is Time.deltaTime doing its job, and you cannot trust the number until you have seen it.Read: the Time.deltaTime row in the quick reference.
  3. Measure what two keys do to one vectorOne print of the movement vector's length: 1 for a single key, 1.414 for two. The bug is a number, not a feeling, and the number is the hypotenuse.Read: the Vector2.magnitude row in the quick reference.
  4. Name the one-line fix, and decide when to take itdirection.normalized rescales any vector to length 1 while keeping its direction, so two keys stop being 41% faster. This lesson names it, shows the line, and does not take it — the file in your project stays as it is.Read: the (a - b).normalized row in the quick reference — direction, length exactly 1.
  5. Choose the number instead of keeping the guessspeed was 4 because that is what the file said when you opened it. Play, change it, and keep the value that suits a world this size.Read: the speed field you wrote in 1.4.

The interesting part is #4. You are going to write down a fix, understand it, and then decide not to apply it — and that decision has to be made by a person who knows what the fix is, not by somebody who never found it. There is a difference between a bug you have not noticed and a debt you have chosen to carry.

Is "which way" still in the same part as "how far"? If you cannot point at the one line where speed is applied, the two are still tangled.

Your turn

The fix is one line and you are not taking it today. Write down what you would tell next week's you, in one sentence, so that the debt does not quietly become a bug nobody remembers.

Name a bug you already shipped in this game that you have noticed and chosen to leave. What made that a decision rather than an oversight?

In the Editor~20 min
  1. Project window → Assets/Scripts, and open PlayerController.cs — the file you built in 1.4.
  2. Game view → press Play and hold D for two seconds, then W and D together for two seconds. Put a landmark on screen and race it. The diagonal covers visibly more ground — you can see the bug before you write anything.
  3. Project window → PlayerController.cs, and read the movement line. xDirection and yDirection are each multiplied by speed. Nothing on that line says how far two of them together are.
  4. Project window → PlayerController.cs, change speed to 2, save, and press Play again. Then 6, or 7. The number lives in the script in this project — tuning is an edit and a new play, not an Inspector box.
  5. GitHub Desktop → commit and push: the two new fields, and the speed you decided on.
Play mode is a dream, edit mode is reality (1.2). A value changed while the Play button is blue resets when you stop — but a value changed in the script is a saved file, and it survives everything.
In the Code~15 min

Unity offers four ways to move an object, each because it handles something the others handle badly. You use the first today.

TechniqueHow it worksNeeds a Rigidbody2D?Best for
transform.Translate(vector)Offsets coordinates directly, skipping the physics engine.NoSimple top-down games, moving UI, linear projectiles
Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position)Drives the body to a target position, so whatever is in the way gets a say: a Dynamic body is stopped by a solid collider, a Kinematic one arrives anyway.Yes — Dynamic if you want a wall to stop itMoving platforms and scripted set pieces that must arrive at an exact position
Rigidbody2D.linearVelocityAssigns a velocity and lets the physics engine move the body. The number is per second, not per frame.Yes — Dynamic if you want a wall to stop itSnappy platformers, arcade physics, momentum across surfaces
Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector)Applies a physical push, factoring in mass, drag and inertia.Yes — Dynamic; a Kinematic body ignores forcesJumping, thrusters, ice physics, knockback
Do not switch methods today. Three of these need a Rigidbody2D your Player does not have, and you will not add one yet: 2.1 adds it for a different purpose (coins) and 2.2 is where it stops you walking through walls.

Socratic: Choosing the Right Tool for the Job

  1. You proved in 1.4 that the translate call walks through walls, while Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position) is stopped by one — on a Dynamic body. What does that call consult that the Transform never does?
  2. Three of these four need a component your Player does not have. What would you add, and where — on the Player, or on the child Sprite?
  3. Why would a spaceship drifting through space prefer Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector) to the translate call?
In the CodeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“why does my character move faster diagonally, and how do I fix it?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. One small change: the two axes get their own fields instead of being multiplied inside the movement line. Everything else in Update() is your 1.4 code, unchanged.

Step 1Give the two axes their own fields

In the class body, under yDirection.

// PlayerController.cs — the class body, below the two direction fields.
    float xVector;
    float yVector;

// PlayerController.cs — inside Update(), after the two reads.
        xVector = xDirection * speed;
        yVector = yDirection * speed;

        transform.Translate(new Vector2(xVector, yVector) * Time.deltaTime);
    }
  1. 2The horizontal part of the movement in units per second. A field rather than a local, because 1.6 reads it to choose an animation and 2.2 hands it to the physics body.
  2. 3The same for vertical. Two numbers that will be handed around as a pair.
  3. 6Turns "pressing right" into "four units per second to the right". Exactly the multiplication 1.4 did inside the move line, moved up and given a name.
  4. 7The same for up/down.
  5. 9The line from 1.4, one term shorter: the speed is already in xVector and yVector, so only the frame time is left to multiply.Say what this line does without reading it aloud: move by (units per second right, units per second up) scaled to the frame I just had. Three separate questions — which way, how fast, how long — and now each one has its own name.
Check your work: the finished filebuild it as you read — then open this to check every line

Compare it against your own file. The difference from 1.4 should be exactly three lines: two fields added, and the multiplication lifted out of the movement line. If you also added a .normalized line, you have taken the fix — that is a defensible choice, and it is not the one this project made today. Be able to say which you did and why.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    float speed = 4;        // units per second — you tune this today

    float xDirection;       // -1, 0 or 1 from the keyboard
    float yDirection;
    float xVector;          // the same thing in units per second
    float yVector;

    void Update()
    {
        xDirection = Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal");
        yDirection = Input.GetAxisRaw("Vertical");

        xVector = xDirection * speed;
        yVector = yDirection * speed;

        transform.Translate(new Vector2(xVector, yVector) * Time.deltaTime);
    }
}
Known Debt: The 41% You Are Not Fixing~20 min

Step 1 — see the number. Add one line to Update(), play, and hold one key, then two: 

        print(new Vector2(xDirection, yDirection).magnitude);

One key reads 1. Two keys read 1.414. That number is √2 — the diagonal of a one-by-one square — and it is exactly why your character covers 41% more ground when you press two keys. Nothing is broken; a vector's length is not the same as its direction, and you have been multiplying speed by a length that changes.

Step 2 — see the one-line fix. This is the line that would remove all 41% of it, in one place, for every direction at once: 

        Vector2 direction = new Vector2(xDirection, yDirection).normalized;

.normalized keeps the arrow pointing the same way and rescales its length to exactly 1. Two keys become (0.707, 0.707) instead of (1, 1), which is still diagonal and still the right shape — 0.707 is 1 ÷ √2. Multiply that by speed and every direction costs the same.

And now the decision: we are not taking it today. This game is top-down, the diagonal is not ruining anything yet, and the fix changes how the character feels — which is the kind of change you want to make on purpose, with a playtest before and after, not at the end of a lesson. So the line is written down here, the debt has a name, and it goes on the board. A known bug you chose is not the same as a bug you never found, and the difference is this paragraph.
Take the print back out. It was an instrument, and it prints once per frame — sixty lines a second — forever. Instruments come out before you commit, or they become the next thing somebody has to debug.

Step 3 — choose the speed. With the debt named, spend the rest of the hour on the number that actually decides how the game feels. speed starts at 4. Try 2, 4, 7: too low is sluggish, too high is twitchy, and there is no correct answer — only the one you can defend against a landmark in your level. Write it down, and say why in one sentence.

Step 4 — catch up. Anyone who has not finished 1.4 or 1.3 uses this time. Anyone who has: place a few landmarks in the Overworld and walk the perimeter, checking the speed against the size of the room the player actually moves in.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Compare four ways to move an object: transform.Translate(vector), Rigidbody2D.MovePosition(position), Rigidbody2D.linearVelocity, Rigidbody2D.AddForce(vector)
  • Say which of the four need a Rigidbody2D, which body type a wall can stop, and what moving along a path does differently from a teleport
  • Explain, in your own words, why (1, 1) is a longer vector than (1, 0) — and what .normalized does about it
  • Say whether your project takes the fix today, and why
  • Explain how Time.deltaTime produces the same real-world speed at different frame rates
  • Pick a speed you can defend, and commit
